job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in data science at Kelburn University, and my day starts with coffee and a coding assistant open before I've even checked my messages. I share a house near campus with three housemates, two of them also coders, and we argue about whose turn it is to do the bins. My parents set money aside for my education from when I was little, so I have no debt, and I use that safety to take risks.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I built a small app for our tenants' union that matches people to repair requests, and I run it on a free server. My bachelor's in software engineering was only a pass, because I spent more time on side projects than on exams. Nobody has hired me yet, but I'm actually fine with that, since I'm still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then we can all stop pretending it's magic and just use the useful parts. I'd probably post a thread online about which tools actually save me time. My housemates would roll their eyes, because I'd have used the assistant to write the thread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan is simple: finish the master's, then get a job at a small company that builds software for public services, like a city council. The assistants save me maybe an hour a day, which is real but not scary. I have over six months saved, and openings in my field around Kelburn are plentiful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the tenants' app and put it in a proper portfolio. I'd apply to around thirty jobs next spring, mostly small firms and city projects. I'd also take a freelance gig or two on the side, because I like the pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little bored, to be honest, because I find the change exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your side projects would count with employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would. My pass degree won't impress anyone, but a working app with real users does. A hiring manager at the council told me last month that she cares more about whether I can ship than about my grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if AI really is just hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go deeper on fundamentals, like databases and testing, which I skipped. Without the hype I'd have to be good at the boring stuff. I'd enjoy that, weirdly, because the assistants never make me understand it.

say: Good, then we can stop pretending it's magic and use the **useful parts**.
I'd post a thread on which tools **actually save time**.
think: My plan is simple: finish the master's and join a small **public-service** software firm.
The assistants save about an hour a day, which is **real but not scary**.
do: Keep building the **tenants' app** and polish it into a portfolio.
Apply to about thirty small firms and city projects, and take a **freelance** gig.
feel: Calm, and a little **bored**, since I like change.
S0.quote: A hiring manager at the council told me last month that she cares more about whether I can ship than about my grades.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on a **working app** with real users, which she thinks counts more than her pass degree.
Already uses AI daily, so 'plateau' is a **mild** world for her, not a disappointing one.

steps.text: Polish the tenants' union app into a public portfolio
Apply to thirty small firms and city projects next spring
Take one or two freelance coding gigs on the side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm excited and a bit guilty about being excited. Online I'd share how I use the tools, and at the union meeting I'd say we need rules on who gets laid off. People should be able to say no to being replaced without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it feels like my moment. Many of the tasks the tools take over are the ones I already use them for, and companies will need people who can direct them. Entry-level jobs will be fewer, but I think I'm in the group who gets one, because I can show working things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and build one big project that uses the tools to do something useful, probably a tenant repair triage for councils. I'd offer it free to two councils as a pilot. I'd also keep teaching my friend Mei, who is on the same course and is nervous, how to use the assistant without copying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with some butterflies. Mostly I feel lucky that I started early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the software take from you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software would take the first drafts of code, the tests and the documentation, and that's what a junior does. So I'd move up to the design and the talking to people. I enjoy talking to the tenants anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in your course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My housemate Dev, who never opens an assistant, and Mei. I'd sit with Dev and show him two tricks a week until he sees it isn't cheating. I think he'd be fine if he started now, but he won't.

say: I'm **excited** and a bit guilty about being excited.
We need rules on who gets **laid off**, with a plan for people replaced.
think: It feels like **my moment**: companies will need people who direct the tools.
Entry jobs will be fewer, but I can **show working things**.
do: Build a big **repair triage** project and offer it free to two councils.
Coach my friend Mei on using the assistant without **copying** it.
feel: Pretty good, with some **butterflies**, and lucky that I started early.
S1.quote: The software would take the first drafts of code, the tests and the documentation, and that's what a junior does.
fieldNote: She is at ease because she already works with the tools, yet she keeps **solidarity** with those who don't.
Turns a threat into a **pilot project** offered to councils for free.

steps.text: Build a repair triage tool and pilot it with two councils
Teach Mei to use the assistant without copying
Show housemate Dev two AI tricks a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should slow this down and put people first. Two years is not enough for schools, the tax system or my parents to adjust. I'd say it loudly on every platform, and I'd help organise a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared. I'm good with the tools, but if AI does any thinking work as well as me by 2028, being good with the tools isn't a job. The jobs I train for could be the first to be gone, right when I finish the master's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself at it. I'd launch the repair app as a real nonprofit-style service, ask the union for a small grant, and apply for any job that touches things people still do with their hands or in person. I'd also learn a trade skill, maybe electrical installation, over a few weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also weirdly awake. I can't sleep, though, because I do the maths on how many entry jobs exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it, mostly. Six months of savings is my freedom. I might spend a little on a course in solar installation, but I wouldn't buy anything big until I could see which jobs are left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the future still seems certain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What seems certain is that people will still need care, repairs and people to organise them. That's why the tenants' union work feels like the safest thing I do. It's connecting neighbours, and no model can sit in a stairwell and listen to a landlord's complaints.

say: Two years is **not enough** for schools, taxes or my parents to adjust.
I'd say it loudly and help organise a **demonstration**.
think: If AI does thinking work as well as me by 2028, being good with the tools **isn't a job**.
My training could be the **first to go**, right when I finish.
do: Launch the repair app as a **community service** and ask the union for a small grant.
Learn **electrical installation** over a few weekends as a hands-on fallback.
feel: Anxious, but **awake**, and I can't sleep because I count entry jobs.
S2.quote: If AI does any thinking work as well as me by 2028, being good with the tools isn't a job.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** shows: she moves at once to community work and a trade skill rather than waiting.
Draws a line between **thinking work** that may vanish and organising work that needs a person.

steps.text: Launch the repair app as a community service with union backing
Organise a demonstration with the tenants' union
Hold savings until the job market is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to build the safety net, and I'd push the union to ask for retraining rights in every contract. Online I'd share what I learn. At university I'd tell friends to get an actual hands-on skill for a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get a good run: three or four years in a job, building things with the tools, saving. Then the thinking side is automated by 2031 and the robots around 2034. I'd be uneasy but I'd have a plan and a few years of money coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job at a small software firm, ideally in the public sector, and save half my pay. I'd keep the tenants' app alive as my own project. In my second year I'd start a part-time course in building services, like heat pumps, as my second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. Five years feels like a long film where I know the twist is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time make you change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes a lot. With two years I'd panic; with five I can build something, and I'd be the person who's already done a job and has a skill set. I'd spend that time collecting two things: some savings and some ways of making money that don't depend on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says retraining won't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say retraining works if you start before you're desperate. People who wait until the layoff letter come out weaker. I'd tell them to try one course in the next six months, even a bad one, and see how it feels.

say: This is the time to build the **safety net**, with retraining rights in every contract.
I'd tell friends to get a real **hands-on skill** as backup.
think: I'd get three or four **good years** of work and saving before the thinking side is automated.
With a plan and a salary I'd be **uneasy**, not scared.
do: Take a job at a small, ideally **public-sector**, software firm and save half my pay.
Start a part-time **heat pump** course in my second year.
feel: Uneasy, not scared: like a long film where I know the **twist**.
S3.quote: Retraining works if you start before you're desperate. People who wait until the layoff letter come out weaker.
fieldNote: Extra years let her plan a **second skill** in building services while employed.
Speaks to others as an organiser would, urging a **first small step**.

steps.text: Take a job at a small public-sector software firm
Save half of every pay cheque
Start a part-time heat pump installation course in year two
Keep the tenants' app running as a side project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best situation we could ask for, because we can fix schools and the tax system before the shock. I'd say it online and at the union and try to be useful. I'd also tell friends not to waste the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pretty calm. By 2036 I'd have nearly ten years in the industry, savings, and probably a role where I design how people and AI work together. The hands-on robots come around 2039, and by then I'd be thirty-seven, with a few options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at a civic tech firm, then move to a better job after three years. I'd save steadily, buy a small flat, and keep building tools for tenants. I'd learn whatever new models appear, and in the second half of the decade I might start my own small company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. I have time to be nosy about all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, and what later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the job and a good manager. Later I'd consider starting something of my own, probably something helping councils and tenant groups use the tools safely, since that's what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to use the decade to build the boring stuff: retraining funds, a way for people to earn something when work shrinks, and open public tools so firms can't hoard them. I don't need a miracle, only paperwork done on time.

say: It's the **best situation** we could ask for, since we can fix schools and taxes first.
I'd tell friends not to **waste the decade**.
think: By 2036 I'd have ten **years in the industry**, savings and a role designing human-AI work.
Hands-on robots arrive in 2039, and I'd have **options** by then.
do: Join a **civic tech** firm and save steadily towards a small flat.
Consider starting my own **small company** in the second half of the decade.
feel: Calm and **curious**, with time to be nosy about it all.
S4.quote: I don't need a miracle, only paperwork done on time.
fieldNote: The decade makes her **calm** and entrepreneurial, with a vision for civic tech.
Asks for **boring public infrastructure** rather than miracles, which is typical of her organiser streak.

steps.text: Join a civic tech firm and move up within three years
Save steadily towards a small flat
Start a small company helping councils use AI safely
Back public funds for retraining at the ballot box

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have no time to turn a pass degree and a good app into a career, and my parents would have no time either. What would help is a plan that exists before it happens: retraining money, income support and public tools anyone can use.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people like me aren't the whole story. I use these tools all day, and I'm still the one losing sleep. The people who never touched them must feel it even harder.

headlineQuote: I use these tools all day, and I'm still the one losing sleep.
portrait: Esther is a **24-year-old** data science master's student with a pass degree, no debt and a house full of coders.
She uses AI **every day** and built a repair app for her tenants' union.
She is progressive and organises: **unions**, public tools and retraining funds are her answers.
Her mood is calm in most worlds and **anxious** when AGI arrives in two years.
She responds to risk by acting at once: a community service, a **trade skill** and a grant.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she would have no time to turn a pass degree and an app into a career.
whatWouldHelp: A plan that exists **before** it happens: retraining money, income support and open public tools.
